<0>Base UI</0> adds `data-starting-style` and `data-ending-style`, so CSS transitions work for both directions, not only keyframes. The popup stays mounted until the animation ends, then is removed, or hidden if the Portal has `keepMounted`. Its animation guide covers Motion, and says it detects Motion animations that include `opacity`.

<0>Base UI</0> has the same shape: one component, several parts. It adds more public utilities around them, such as `useRender` and `mergeProps`, so you can write your own parts that behave like the built-in ones. It is React-only, built by people who worked on Radix, Material UI and Floating UI.
<0>Base UI</0>: 37 components in its docs index, including Combobox, Autocomplete, Number Field, OTP Field, Drawer, Toast and Preview Card, which Radix doesn't have.
<0>Events bubble through your tree.</0> The UI SDK docs warn that a click handler or a link wrapped around a popup also gets the clicks inside it. Keep popups outside clickable cards.
<0>Fewer wrapper parts.</0> Placement props such as `side`, `align` and `sideOffset` go on the content, not on a Positioner.

<0>Mixing is possible.</0> UI SDK components don't need a provider, so a Base UI app can use a UI SDK Color Picker on one screen. You carry two dependencies and two sets of attribute names, so keep it to the components you can't get elsewhere.
<0>No stacking fights.</0> Top-layer content sits above the page whatever the `z-index` of a sticky header or a transformed parent.

<0>Pick Base UI</0> for a new React design system you want to ship on stable APIs this quarter. It is the default under new shadcn/ui projects, covers more components than Radix and uses the attribute model most of the ecosystem is moving to.
<0>Pick Radix</0> if you have a working Radix codebase, your team knows it, and you don't need a component it lacks. It is stable, React-only and MIT.

<0>Pick UI SDK</0> if you need more than React, want components such as Color Picker, Date Picker or Tree without a second library, or want AI agents to operate your UI through structured tools. Accept that it is a beta.

<0>Radix</0> animates mount and unmount with CSS animations on `data-state`. Its docs say it suspends unmount while the exit animation plays. For JavaScript animation libraries, many parts accept `forceMount` so the library decides when children mount.

<0>Radix</0> ships one primitive per component. A Dialog package gives you Root, Trigger, Portal, Overlay, Content, Title, Description and Close, and that is the unit you work with. The behaviors inside, like focus trapping and dismissal, are internal. The `radix-ui` package bundles them all.
<0>Radix</0>: 30 primitive packages in `radix-ui` 1.8.1, from Accordion to Tooltip, plus utilities like Slot, Portal and Visually Hidden.

<0>Start on Base UI</0> when you are building a React component library or a product UI to ship now. It is stable, it is shadcn/ui's default, and its popups, forms and animation patterns are well documented.

<0>Stay on Radix</0> when the app works, the team knows it, and you aren't blocked. Nothing here forces a move. If you do move, move to Base UI first: it is the smaller step, and the attribute model you learn transfers to UI SDK.

<0>UI SDK</0> splits the layers differently. `@ui-sdk/core` is a TypeScript library of behaviors: roving focus, typeahead, popups, drag and drop, announcements and many more. A primitive combines behaviors with state and named slots through `definePrimitive`. The components you import from `@ui-sdk/react` are primitives rendered by the React adapter, and the same primitives render in Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components through their adapters. Its docs pitch this at agents: give an agent tested behaviors and it can build a component the library doesn't ship, like an icon picker or a kanban board.

<0>UI SDK</0> uses the same two attributes with the same meaning. Content stays mounted until its exit transition or animation finishes, `keepMounted` keeps closed content in the page, and `onOpenChangeComplete` runs when the open or close is done. The UI SDK docs don't have a guide for Motion yet, beyond a note to use `keepMounted` when an animation library needs closed content to stay in the DOM.
<0>UI SDK</0>: 55 components and two hooks in the docs bundled with 0.1.0-beta.1.

The `data-slot` row matters more than it looks. shadcn/ui adds its own `data-slot` attributes in its wrapper files, because Radix and Base UI don't emit one. In my scratch app, the Base UI popup carried `data-open`, `data-side` and `data-align`, and no `data-slot`. UI SDK sets it on every part itself, like `data-slot="popover-content"`, and the docs treat it as a managed attribute your props can't override. That gives global CSS and agents a stable name for each part.

This is the part only UI SDK has. `createAgent()` from `@ui-sdk/react/agent` connects to every UI SDK component on the page. `snapshot()` lists them with their labels, state and available actions. `act()` calls those actions through each component's API, and your change callbacks see `details.source === "agent"`. `registerTools()` offers the same tools to an agent built into the browser through WebMCP.

UI SDK vs Base UI vs Radix: which to pick
UI SDK's React package requires React 19 and React DOM 19 or newer, with `@types/react` 19.2.10 or newer. If you are still on React 18, that decides it for now.

Until this week, picking the primitive layer under a shadcn/ui-style component library meant picking between two options: Radix and Base UI. On 12 November 2026 Vercel Labs published a third, UI SDK, as `0.1.0-beta.1`. It is headless like the other two, but it is built around a different idea, and it ships something neither of them has: a bridge that lets AI agents read and operate the components.

Vercel's docs include a benchmark of that difference on a project-settings task. By their numbers, with Sonnet through Claude Code and medians of three runs, the agent bridge cut tool calls from 16 to 5 and cost from $0.073 to $0.032. Those are Vercel's figures for one task, not mine, but the direction makes sense: reading a list of components with their state is cheaper than reading a page. I built a working demo of the bridge, with permissions and a custom component, in <0>Make your React app operable by AI agents</0>.
